tutorials.title: Sex-Linked Inheritance
tutorials.body: Sex-linked genes sit on the X or Y chromosome, so they are inherited along with biological sex. Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on it, such as the one for red-green color blindness, shows up with no second copy to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes and usually need both copies to be recessive, which is why X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males.

tutorials.title: Polygenic Traits
tutorials.body: A polygenic trait is controlled by many genes acting together, so instead of a few distinct categories you get a smooth range of outcomes. Human height and skin color work this way, which is why a class of people forms a bell-shaped spread rather than just tall or short. A single Punnett square cannot capture this, because each gene adds a small amount to the total effect.

tutorials.title: Pleiotropy
tutorials.body: Pleiotropy is when a single gene affects several seemingly unrelated traits at once. The same gene change can ripple into many body systems because its protein is used in more than one place. In sickle cell disease, for example, one altered gene changes the shape of red blood cells, which in turn affects oxygen delivery, pain, organ function, and even resistance to malaria.

tutorials.title: Epistasis
tutorials.body: Epistasis is when one gene masks or overrides the effect of a completely different gene. A common example is coat color in Labrador retrievers: one gene decides whether the pigment is black or brown, but a second gene can switch pigment off entirely and produce a yellow lab regardless of what the first gene says. So a dog can carry black-coat alleles yet still be yellow because the masking gene won out.

tutorials.title: The 3:1 Monohybrid Ratio
tutorials.body: When you cross two heterozygotes for one trait, such as Bb crossed with Bb, the four-box Punnett square gives one BB, two Bb, and one bb. Because both BB and Bb show the dominant trait, three of the four boxes look dominant and only one looks recessive, producing the famous 3:1 phenotype ratio. The genotype ratio underneath is actually 1:2:1, which is hidden because the heterozygotes look just like the dominant homozygotes.

tutorials.title: Linkage and Crossing Over
tutorials.body: Genes that sit close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited as a package, which is called linkage, so they break the usual independent-assortment rules behind Punnett squares. During the formation of egg and sperm cells, matching chromosomes can swap matching segments in a process called crossing over, which shuffles alleles and can separate even linked genes. The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the less often crossing over splits them apart.

tutorials.title: Genotype vs. Phenotype
tutorials.body: The genotype is the actual set of alleles an organism carries, while the phenotype is the trait you can observe, such as eye color or height. The same phenotype can come from different genotypes, because a dominant trait shows up whether you have one or two dominant alleles. That is exactly why a Punnett square's genotype ratio of 1:2:1 collapses into a 3:1 phenotype ratio, and why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

tutorials.title: Seafloor Spreading
tutorials.body: At mid-ocean ridges, two plates pull apart and hot rock rises from the mantle to fill the gap, cooling into fresh seafloor that pushes the older crust outward on both sides. This means the ocean floor is youngest right at the ridge and gets steadily older the farther away you look. Picture a conveyor belt: new material is added in the middle and carried sideways, slowly widening the ocean over millions of years. This is part of why the Atlantic Ocean is still getting a little wider every year.

tutorials.title: Subduction Zones
tutorials.body: Where two plates collide and one is denser, the heavier plate bends and sinks beneath the lighter one back down into the mantle. As the sinking slab heats up, it releases water that lowers the melting point of the rock above it, feeding chains of volcanoes near the boundary. Think of pushing one edge of a floating rug under another until it slips below the surface. This is why volcanoes and deep ocean trenches often line up along the same coastlines.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why oceanic crust subducts under continental crust and not the other way around.

tutorials.title: Transform Faults
tutorials.body: A transform fault is a boundary where two plates grind horizontally past each other instead of pulling apart or colliding, so no crust is created or destroyed. The rough surfaces snag and build up strain until they suddenly slip, which is what produces earthquakes there. It is like two bricks sliding past one another with their gritty faces catching, then jerking free. The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example separating two plates moving in opposite directions.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why transform faults usually don't make volcanoes.

tutorials.title: Convergent Boundaries
tutorials.body: A convergent boundary is where two plates move toward each other, and what happens depends on what kinds of crust meet. Ocean-meets-ocean or ocean-meets-continent leads to subduction and volcanic arcs, while continent-meets-continent crumples both edges upward because neither is dense enough to sink. The result can be towering mountain ranges, deep trenches, or strings of volcanoes. It is like two cars in a head-on collision: the metal has nowhere to go but up and outward.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me which kind of convergent boundary built the Himalayas.

tutorials.title: Divergent Boundaries
tutorials.body: A divergent boundary is where two plates move away from each other, letting hot mantle rock rise and create brand-new crust in the gap. Under the ocean this builds mid-ocean ridges, and on land it forms rift valleys where the ground stretches, thins, and drops down between cracks. Imagine slowly pulling apart a stretched piece of taffy until the middle thins and tears. East Africa is being torn apart this way right now and may eventually split off into a new sea.

tutorials.title: Ridge Push and Slab Pull
tutorials.body: Plates don't just drift randomly; two forces do most of the pushing and pulling. Ridge push happens because the elevated, hot rock at a mid-ocean ridge slides downhill and shoves the plate away, while slab pull happens when a cold, dense subducting slab sinks and drags the rest of the plate behind it like a tablecloth slipping off a table. Slab pull is generally considered the stronger of the two. Underlying mantle convection helps, but these edge forces dominate the motion of a plate.

tutorials.title: Hotspots and Mantle Plumes
tutorials.body: A hotspot is a fixed column of unusually hot rock rising from deep in the mantle that melts through the plate above it, creating volcanoes far from any plate boundary. Because the plume stays roughly in place while the plate slides over it, it punches out a trail of volcanoes, with the oldest ones carried farthest away and the active one sitting over the plume now. Think of holding a candle under a sheet of paper you slowly drag across it, leaving a line of scorch marks. The Hawaiian island chain formed exactly this way.

tutorials.title: The Wadati-Benioff Zone
tutorials.body: A Wadati-Benioff zone is the sloping band of earthquakes that traces a subducting slab as it dives deeper into the mantle. The quakes get progressively deeper the farther you move inland from the trench, mapping out the angle and path of the descending plate even though we can't see it directly. It is like dropping a marked stick into murky water and tracking it only by the bubbles rising along its length. These deep quake patterns gave early scientists some of the first clear proof that whole slabs really sink into the mantle.

tutorials.title: Isostasy
tutorials.body: Isostasy is the idea that the rigid plates float on the denser, slowly flowing mantle beneath them, finding a balance like ice cubes bobbing in water. Thicker or lighter crust rides higher and also pushes a deeper root down below, which is why tall mountain ranges have thick crustal roots underneath them. When a heavy ice sheet melts away, the land it was pressing down slowly rebounds upward over thousands of years. Parts of Scandinavia and Canada are still rising today for exactly that reason.

tutorials.title: Accretionary Wedge
tutorials.body: An accretionary wedge is a pile of seafloor sediment and rock that gets scraped off a subducting plate and plastered onto the edge of the overriding plate. As the lower plate dives down, the soft material on top is shaved off and stacked into a wedge-shaped, folded heap near the trench. Picture a snowplow pushing snow into a growing ridge in front of its blade. Over time these wedges can grow large enough to become dry land or even contribute to building coastal mountains.

tutorials.title: Triple Junctions
tutorials.body: A triple junction is a point where three tectonic plate boundaries meet, so three plates share a single corner. The boundaries can be any mix of ridges, trenches, and transform faults, and some combinations are stable and stay put while others slowly migrate over time. Think of the spot where three slices of a pie all come to a point in the center. The Afar region in East Africa sits near such a junction, where rifting in several directions is pulling the crust apart at once.

tutorials.title: The Wilson Cycle
tutorials.body: The Wilson cycle describes the long-term life story of an ocean basin: continents rift apart, a new ocean opens and widens through seafloor spreading, then subduction begins, the ocean closes, and finally the continents collide to raise mountains. The cycle can take hundreds of millions of years to run its course before starting over. It is like a slow breath in and out, with oceans being born, growing, and disappearing again. The Atlantic is currently in its opening stage while remnants of older closed oceans are recorded inside mountain belts like the Appalachians.

tutorials.title: Sonic Boom
tutorials.body: A sonic boom is the loud crack you hear when an object travels faster than the speed of sound. The object outruns its own pressure waves, so those waves pile up into a single sharp shock front shaped like a cone trailing behind it. When that cone sweeps over your ears, all the built-up pressure arrives at once as a bang. A supersonic jet doesn't boom only when it 'breaks the barrier' — it drags the boom along the ground the whole time it's flying that fast.

tutorials.title: Mach Number and the Sound Barrier
tutorials.body: The Mach number is an object's speed divided by the local speed of sound, so Mach 1 means moving exactly as fast as sound travels in that air. The 'sound barrier' isn't a wall — it's the sharp rise in air resistance that happens as an aircraft approaches Mach 1, because the air can't get out of the way fast enough and pressure waves stack up in front. Above Mach 1 the craft is supersonic and outruns its own sound. Because the speed of sound drops in colder, thinner high-altitude air, the same true speed can be a higher Mach number up high than at sea level.

tutorials.title: Why Decibels Are Logarithmic
tutorials.body: Human hearing spans an enormous range of sound intensities, so loudness is measured on the decibel scale, which is logarithmic rather than linear. Each increase of about ten decibels represents roughly ten times more sound intensity, even though our ears perceive it as only 'about twice as loud.' That's why a whisper and a jet engine can be described with numbers that look close together but differ by trillions in actual energy. It also means two identical sound sources together are only about three decibels louder than one, not double the decibel number.

tutorials.title: Beat Frequency
tutorials.body: When two sounds of slightly different frequencies play together, they drift in and out of step, alternately reinforcing and cancelling each other. The result is a slow throbbing in loudness called a beat, and the number of throbs per second equals the difference between the two frequencies. Musicians use this to tune instruments: as two strings get closer in pitch, the beats slow down, and when the wobble disappears entirely the notes match. You can hear it as a 'wah-wah-wah' pulse when two people hum almost-but-not-quite the same note.

tutorials.title: Sound Diffraction
tutorials.body: Diffraction is the way waves bend around edges and spread out after passing through gaps, and sound does it readily because its wavelengths are large — often comparable to the size of everyday doorways and walls. That bending is why you can hear someone talking in the next room even when you can't see them around the corner. Low, long-wavelength sounds like bass diffract more than high, short-wavelength sounds, which is part of why you mainly hear the thumping bass from a party down the street while the crisp treble is lost.

tutorials.title: Refraction of Sound Through Air Layers
tutorials.body: Sound travels faster in warmer air, so when air temperature changes with height, sound waves bend toward the cooler, slower layers. On a sunny day the ground is hot and the air above is cooler, so sound bends upward and away from a listener, making distant sounds fade quickly. At night the ground cools and a warm layer sits above, so sound bends back down toward the ground and carries much farther. That's why a train horn or distant voices can sound surprisingly clear across a lake on a calm evening.

tutorials.title: Acoustic Impedance
tutorials.body: Acoustic impedance describes how much a material resists being set into vibration by a sound wave, and it depends on the material's density and the speed of sound within it. When a sound wave hits a boundary between two materials with very different impedances, most of the energy reflects instead of crossing over. That's why sound made in air mostly bounces off a water surface rather than entering it, and why ultrasound machines use a gel to bridge the impedance gap between the probe and your skin so the sound can get inside.

tutorials.title: Reverberation
tutorials.body: Reverberation is the lingering wash of sound that remains after a source stops, made of countless reflections bouncing off walls, floors, and ceilings and arriving at your ears slightly delayed. Unlike a distinct echo, these reflections blur together into a smooth tail because each surface sends sound back many times. Hard, bare rooms reverberate a lot and sound boomy, while curtains, carpet, and furniture absorb the energy and deaden it. Concert halls are tuned for just enough reverberation to make music feel rich without smearing the notes together.

tutorials.title: Moving Source vs Moving Observer
tutorials.body: The Doppler effect for sound is not perfectly symmetric: it matters whether the source is moving or the listener is, because sound travels through air, which acts as a fixed reference medium. A moving source bunches up the actual wave crests in front of it, while a moving listener simply runs into or away from crests faster. At everyday speeds the two cases give almost the same pitch shift, but the underlying math differs slightly. This is unlike the Doppler effect for light, where only the relative motion matters because light needs no medium.

tutorials.title: Doppler Radar
tutorials.body: Doppler radar bounces radio waves off a moving target and measures how the reflected wave's frequency has shifted, using that shift to calculate the target's speed toward or away from the device. A police speed gun does this to a passing car, while weather radar uses it to see how fast rain and wind are moving inside a storm, revealing rotation that can signal a tornado. Because it relies on the Doppler shift, it measures only the part of the motion along the radar beam, so a car crossing sideways would barely register.

tutorials.title: Relativistic Doppler Effect
tutorials.body: For light from very fast-moving sources, the ordinary Doppler shift is modified by special relativity, because the source's clock runs slow from the observer's point of view. This adds an extra time-dilation factor on top of the usual frequency change, and it even produces a transverse Doppler shift — a redshift you see when the source moves straight across your line of sight, where classical theory predicts no shift at all. Astronomers must use these relativistic formulas when measuring the speeds of distant galaxies and fast jets of matter near black holes.

tutorials.title: What Sets the Speed of Sound in a Material
tutorials.body: The speed of sound in a material depends on two competing properties: its stiffness, which speeds sound up, and its density, which slows it down. Solids like steel are extremely stiff, so even though they are dense, sound races through them many times faster than through air. This is why you can hear a distant train sooner by pressing your ear to the rail than by listening through the air. It also explains why sound is faster in water than in air but slower in lead than in aluminum, since stiffness usually wins out over density.

tutorials.title: Active Noise Cancellation
tutorials.body: Active noise-cancelling headphones use a tiny microphone to listen to incoming sound, then play back a matching wave that is exactly inverted — its peaks line up with the noise's troughs. When the two waves meet, they undergo destructive interference and largely cancel, leaving near silence. This works best on steady low-frequency drones like an airplane engine, because the headphones can predict and invert that smooth wave; sudden, high-pitched sounds are too quick and irregular to cancel cleanly. It's the same wave-cancelling idea as beats, but aimed at erasing sound rather than making it pulse.

tutorials.title: Induced Fit vs Lock-and-Key
tutorials.body: The old lock-and-key idea pictured an enzyme's active site as a rigid slot the substrate slips into. The induced-fit model is closer to reality: the active site is flexible and reshapes itself slightly around the substrate once it arrives, gripping it and straining its bonds toward the reaction. It is less like a stiff lock and more like a hand closing around a ball it has just caught.

tutorials.title: Cofactors and Coenzymes
tutorials.body: Many enzymes can't work alone and need a non-protein helper called a cofactor. Cofactors that are metal ions (like zinc or iron) lock into the enzyme, while organic helpers are called coenzymes, several of which your body builds from vitamins. The bare protein is the apoenzyme; add its cofactor and you get the active holoenzyme. This is one reason vitamin deficiencies can stall whole chunks of your metabolism.

tutorials.title: Competitive Inhibition
tutorials.body: A competitive inhibitor is a molecule shaped enough like the real substrate to slot into the active site, where it just sits and blocks the substrate from binding. Because it competes for the same spot, flooding the cell with more substrate can outcompete it and restore the reaction. Many drugs work this way, jamming an enzyme's active site so its normal job slows down.

tutorials.title: Allosteric Regulation
tutorials.body: Some enzymes have a second binding spot away from the active site called an allosteric site. When a regulator molecule docks there, it bends the whole protein into a different shape, turning the active site on or off without touching it directly. This lets cells dial enzymes up or down on the fly, like a thermostat that responds to how much product has already piled up.

tutorials.title: Feedback Inhibition
tutorials.body: In a chain of reactions where each enzyme hands its product to the next, the final product often loops back and switches off the first enzyme in the line. That way the cell stops spending raw materials the moment it has made enough, then resumes when stocks run low. It is the same logic as a factory that pauses the assembly line once the warehouse is full.

tutorials.title: Temperature, pH, and Denaturation
tutorials.body: Every enzyme has a sweet spot of temperature and pH where its precise folded shape works best. Push the heat or acidity too far and the protein unravels, a permanent change called denaturation that wrecks the active site. It is exactly what happens when you fry an egg: the heat denatures its proteins, and they never go back to clear and runny.

tutorials.title: Glycolysis
tutorials.body: Glycolysis is the opening act of breaking down sugar: a chain of enzymes splits one glucose into two smaller pyruvate molecules right in the cell's cytoplasm. It spends a little energy up front to gain more back, netting a small amount of ATP plus electron carriers for later stages. Crucially it needs no oxygen, which is why it is the oldest and most universal energy trick in life.

tutorials.title: The Citric Acid Cycle
tutorials.body: Also called the Krebs cycle, this is a loop of reactions in the mitochondria that finishes pulling apart the carbons from food. Each turn strips off carbon dioxide you breathe out and loads up electron carriers that feed the next stage. Think of it as the spinning gear that doesn't make much energy directly but charges up the batteries the cell will cash in afterward.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what is the electron transport chain?'

tutorials.title: The Electron Transport Chain
tutorials.body: This is where cells make the bulk of their ATP. Electron carriers charged up earlier dump their electrons into a row of proteins in the mitochondrial membrane, and the energy released pumps protons to one side. Those protons then rush back through a turbine-like enzyme that spins to crank out ATP, a process called chemiosmosis. Oxygen sits at the very end to grab the spent electrons, which is the whole reason you need to breathe.

tutorials.title: ATP Synthase
tutorials.body: ATP synthase is a tiny molecular motor embedded in the mitochondrial membrane. Protons crowded on one side flow back through it like water through a dam, physically spinning part of the enzyme. That rotation snaps a phosphate onto ADP to build ATP, the cell's rechargeable energy battery. It is one of the few cases in biology where you can literally call a protein a spinning turbine.

tutorials.title: Fermentation
tutorials.body: When oxygen runs short, cells can't finish the usual energy chain, so they fall back on fermentation to keep glycolysis running. In your muscles, hard sprinting builds up lactic acid this way, contributing to that burning, tired feeling. Yeast does a different version, turning sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is exactly how bread rises and beer brews.

tutorials.title: Anabolism vs Catabolism
tutorials.body: Your metabolism runs two opposite directions at once. Catabolism breaks big molecules down into smaller ones and releases energy, like digesting a meal into usable fuel. Anabolism spends that energy to build big molecules up, like knitting amino acids into the muscle you grow after a workout. Tearing down and building up are constantly traded off depending on whether you've just eaten or are running on reserves.

how body makes sugar when fasting
tutorials.title: Gluconeogenesis
tutorials.body: When you haven't eaten and blood sugar dips, your liver builds fresh glucose from non-sugar sources like amino acids and lactate. It is roughly glycolysis run in reverse, but it uses a few different enzymes to push past the steps that normally only flow one way. This is what keeps your brain, a glucose hog, fueled through an overnight fast or a long stretch without food.

tutorials.title: Deposition (Gas to Solid)
tutorials.body: Deposition is when a gas turns straight into a solid without ever passing through the liquid stage, the exact reverse of sublimation. The vapor particles lose energy and lock into a solid arrangement all at once instead of first puddling into a liquid. Frost on a cold window or on the grass is the classic example: water vapor in the air freezes directly onto the chilly surface as delicate ice crystals.

tutorials.title: The Triple Point
tutorials.body: The triple point is the single, exact combination of temperature and pressure where a substance can exist as solid, liquid, and gas all at the same time, in balance. At that precise point ice, water, and steam can sit together in the same container without any one of them winning out. It is so reliable and reproducible that scientists long used water's triple point to help define the temperature scale itself.
tutorials.tryIt: Try asking: what is a supercritical fluid

tutorials.title: Supercritical Fluids
tutorials.body: Push a substance past its critical point, a special temperature and pressure, and the difference between liquid and gas simply disappears, leaving a single state called a supercritical fluid. It can flow and fill a container like a gas but dissolve things like a liquid, blurring the usual boundary. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used industrially to decaffeinate coffee beans, since it soaks out the caffeine but leaves no harmful residue behind.

tutorials.title: Plasma: The Fourth State of Matter
tutorials.body: Heat a gas hot enough, or zap it with strong energy, and electrons get torn away from their atoms, leaving a glowing soup of charged particles called plasma. Because it is full of free charges, plasma conducts electricity and bends to magnetic fields in ways an ordinary gas cannot. You meet it every day in lightning, neon signs, and the flickering glow of the Sun, which is itself an enormous ball of plasma.

tutorials.title: Bose-Einstein Condensate
tutorials.body: A Bose-Einstein condensate is an exotic state that forms when certain atoms are cooled to a whisker above absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible. At that point the atoms slow almost to a standstill and merge into one shared quantum blob, all behaving as a single entity rather than as separate particles. It is the opposite extreme from plasma: where plasma is matter at scorching energy, this is matter at the very bottom of the cold.

tutorials.title: Surface Tension
tutorials.body: Inside a liquid every molecule is pulled in all directions by its neighbors, but at the surface there are no neighbors above, so those molecules pull sideways and inward, forming a kind of stretchy skin. This is why water beads up into round droplets and why a gently placed paper clip or a water strider can rest on the surface without sinking. It also pulls small drops into the most compact shape possible, a sphere.

tutorials.title: Viscosity
tutorials.body: Viscosity is a liquid's resistance to flowing, set by how strongly its particles cling to and drag past one another. Thick, sticky liquids like honey or syrup have high viscosity and ooze slowly, while thin liquids like water have low viscosity and pour fast. Warming a liquid usually lowers its viscosity, which is why honey runs much more easily after you heat it.

tutorials.title: Boiling Point and Pressure
tutorials.body: A liquid boils when its escaping vapor pushes hard enough to match the air pressure pressing down on it, so lower air pressure lets it boil at a lower temperature. On a high mountain the thinner air means water boils well below its sea-level temperature, so cooking takes longer because the water is cooler. A pressure cooker does the opposite: it traps steam to raise the pressure, letting water get hotter than usual and cook food faster.

tutorials.title: Supercooling
tutorials.body: Supercooling is when a very pure, undisturbed liquid is chilled below its normal freezing point yet stays liquid, because it has no speck or jolt to trigger the first crystals. Freezing usually needs a starting point such as a dust grain or a scratch, and without one the molecules cannot get organized. A bottle of very clean water can sometimes be cooled below freezing and then snap into ice the instant you tap it or drop in a single crystal.

tutorials.title: Inertia
tutorials.body: Inertia is the lazy streak in everything: an object keeps doing what it's already doing unless a force changes it. A still object stays still, and a moving one keeps moving in a straight line. The more mass something has, the more inertia it has, so heavy things are harder to start or stop.
tutorials.example: When a bus stops suddenly, your body lurches forward because your inertia keeps you moving even though the bus stopped.

tutorials.title: Newton's First Law
tutorials.body: Newton's first law says an object won't change its motion unless a force pushes or pulls it. No force? Then a resting thing stays at rest and a moving thing keeps gliding at the same speed and direction. Forces are what make things speed up, slow down, or turn.
tutorials.example: A hockey puck on smooth ice slides for a long time because almost no force slows it down.

tutorials.title: Net Force
tutorials.body: When several forces push on one object, you add them up (counting direction) to get the net force. That single combined force decides what happens. If the forces cancel out, the net force is zero and motion doesn't change. If they don't cancel, the object accelerates in the leftover direction.
tutorials.example: In tug-of-war, if both teams pull equally hard the rope doesn't move because the net force is zero.

tutorials.title: Balanced vs Unbalanced Forces
tutorials.body: Balanced forces are evenly matched, so they cancel and the object's motion stays the same. Unbalanced forces don't cancel, leaving a net force that changes the motion, making the object speed up, slow down, or change direction. Only unbalanced forces cause acceleration.
tutorials.example: A book resting on a table has gravity pulling down and the table pushing up equally, so forces are balanced and it stays put.

tutorials.title: Static vs Kinetic Friction
tutorials.body: Static friction holds a still object in place and must be overcome before it starts sliding. Once it's moving, kinetic friction takes over and is usually a bit weaker. That's why something is harder to get moving than to keep moving.
tutorials.example: It takes a big shove to start a heavy couch sliding, but once it's moving it slides more easily.

tutorials.title: Air Resistance
tutorials.body: Air resistance is friction from air pushing back on things moving through it. The faster you go and the bigger your surface facing the air, the stronger it gets. It's why a feather flutters down slowly while a rock drops fast, and why parachutes work.
tutorials.example: Sticking your hand out a moving car window, you feel the air pushing it back.

tutorials.title: Mass vs Weight
tutorials.body: Mass is how much stuff is in an object and never changes no matter where you are. Weight is how hard gravity pulls on that mass, so weight changes with gravity. On the Moon your mass stays the same, but you weigh about six times less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
tutorials.example: An astronaut with the same mass on Earth and the Moon weighs much less on the Moon.

tutorials.title: Speed vs Velocity
tutorials.body: Speed tells you how fast something moves. Velocity tells you how fast AND which direction. So two cars going 50 km/h have the same speed, but if one heads north and one heads south, they have different velocities. Direction is the key difference.
tutorials.example: A car driving in a circle at a steady 30 km/h has constant speed but changing velocity because its direction keeps turning.

tutorials.title: Circular Motion
tutorials.body: Circular motion is when something travels along a curved path around a center point. Even at constant speed, it's always accelerating because its direction keeps changing. A force pointing toward the center is what keeps bending the path into a circle.
tutorials.example: The Moon stays in circular motion around Earth because gravity keeps pulling it inward.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is moving in a circle always accelerating?'

tutorials.title: Projectile Motion
tutorials.body: When you throw something, it moves forward and falls down at the same time. Its forward motion stays steady while gravity pulls it down faster and faster, bending the path into a smooth curved arc. That curve is why everything thrown eventually comes back down.
tutorials.example: A thrown basketball arcs up, slows at the top, then curves down into the hoop.

tutorials.title: Normal Force
tutorials.body: The normal force is the push a surface gives back to an object resting on it, pointing straight away from the surface. It's why you don't sink through the floor: the floor pushes up just as hard as gravity pulls you down, balancing things out.
tutorials.example: A book on a table is held up by the table's normal force pushing up on it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what stops me from falling through the floor?'

tutorials.title: Tension
tutorials.body: Tension is the pulling force carried along a rope, string, or cable when it's stretched tight. It pulls equally on whatever is attached at both ends. A rope can only pull, never push, so tension always points along the rope away from the object.
tutorials.example: In tug-of-war, the tight rope carries tension that pulls on both teams.

tutorials.title: Hooke's Law
tutorials.body: Hooke's law says a spring's pull-back force grows in step with how far you stretch or squash it. Pull twice as far and it pulls back twice as hard. This works only up to a point; stretch too far and the spring bends out of shape and stops obeying the rule.
tutorials.example: A bathroom scale uses a spring that squashes more as you weigh more, showing your weight.

tutorials.title: Power (Physics)
tutorials.body: Power is how fast energy is used or work is done. Doing the same job quickly takes more power than doing it slowly. Two engines might do the same total work, but the more powerful one finishes sooner. Power is measured in watts.
tutorials.example: Running up the stairs uses more power than walking up, even though the work done is the same.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what's the difference between energy and power?'

tutorials.title: Insulation
tutorials.body: Insulation slows the flow of heat by using materials that conduct poorly, often trapping pockets of air. Trapped air is a great insulator because it doesn't move heat easily. That's why fluffy coats, foam, and double windows keep warmth where you want it.
tutorials.example: A puffy jacket keeps you warm by trapping air that slows heat escaping from your body.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a fluffy coat keep me warm?'

tutorials.title: Waves
tutorials.body: A wave is a traveling disturbance that carries energy from place to place without moving the material itself very far. The water or rope just wiggles up and down or back and forth while the energy moves through it. Sound, light, and ripples are all waves.
tutorials.example: A floating duck bobs in place as ocean waves pass under it; the wave moves but the water mostly stays put.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'does a wave carry water across the ocean?'

tutorials.title: Transverse Waves
tutorials.body: In a transverse wave, the material wiggles up and down (or side to side) while the wave travels at a right angle to that wiggle. Light and the wave you make by shaking a rope are transverse. The crests and troughs are the high and low points.
tutorials.example: Shake one end of a rope up and down and a transverse wave travels along it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'which way do the bits move in a rope wave?'

tutorials.title: Longitudinal Waves
tutorials.body: In a longitudinal wave, the material squishes and stretches back and forth in the same direction the wave travels, making compressions and rarefactions. Sound is the classic example, pushing air particles forward and back.
tutorials.example: Push and pull a slinky along its length and you see compressions travel down it like sound through air.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how does a slinky show a sound wave?'

tutorials.title: Frequency
tutorials.body: Frequency is how many wave cycles pass a point each second, measured in hertz. High frequency means lots of fast wiggles; low frequency means few slow ones. For sound, higher frequency means higher pitch.
tutorials.example: A high-pitched whistle has a higher frequency than a deep drum.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what makes a sound high or low pitched?'

tutorials.title: Amplitude
tutorials.body: Amplitude is how big a wave is, measured from the calm middle to a peak. Bigger amplitude means more energy. For sound that means louder; for light it means brighter. The wiggle's height, not its spacing, sets the amplitude.
tutorials.example: Shouting makes sound waves with bigger amplitude than whispering, so they sound louder.

tutorials.title: Wave Speed
tutorials.body: Wave speed is how fast a wave's energy travels through a material. It depends mostly on what the wave is moving through, not on how hard you make the wave. Sound zips faster through water and solids than through air.
tutorials.example: Sound travels much faster through a metal rail than through the air, so you'd hear it through the rail first.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'does sound travel faster in air or water?'

tutorials.title: Reflection
tutorials.body: Reflection is when a wave bounces off a surface instead of passing through. Light reflecting lets you see things and makes mirrors work; sound reflecting makes echoes. The wave bounces off at the same angle it hit, like a ball off a wall.
tutorials.example: A mirror works because light bounces off its smooth shiny surface back to your eyes.

tutorials.title: Refraction
tutorials.body: Refraction is the bending of a wave as it passes from one material into another and changes speed. Light slows down entering water and bends, which is why a straw in a glass looks broken at the surface.
tutorials.example: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the waterline because light refracts as it leaves the water.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a straw look bent in water?'

tutorials.title: Diffraction
tutorials.body: Diffraction is how waves spread out and bend around edges or through gaps. It's why you can hear someone around a corner even when you can't see them: sound waves bend around the corner more easily than light does.
tutorials.example: You can hear a voice from around a corner because sound waves diffract around the edge.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why can I hear around corners but not see around them?'

tutorials.title: Interference
tutorials.body: When two waves overlap, they add together. Crests meeting crests make a bigger wave (constructive), while a crest meeting a trough can cancel out (destructive). This combining is called interference and explains everything from louder spots to noise-canceling headphones.
tutorials.example: Noise-canceling headphones make an opposite sound wave to cancel out unwanted noise.

tutorials.title: Sound
tutorials.body: Sound is a wave made of vibrations traveling through a material, usually air. A vibrating object pushes and pulls the air, sending ripples of pressure to your ears. No material means no sound, which is why space is silent.
tutorials.example: A drum makes sound because its skin vibrates and shakes the air around it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is there no sound in space?'

tutorials.title: Pitch
tutorials.body: Pitch is how high or low a sound seems, and it depends on the sound wave's frequency. Fast vibrations make high-pitched sounds; slow vibrations make low ones. Tightening or shortening a string raises its pitch by speeding up its vibration.
tutorials.example: A tightly stretched guitar string vibrates faster and plays a higher note.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a thinner string sound higher?'

tutorials.title: Loudness
tutorials.body: Loudness is how strong a sound seems, and it depends on the sound wave's amplitude, or how much energy it carries. Bigger vibrations move more air and sound louder. Loudness is measured in decibels, and very loud sounds can damage your ears.
tutorials.example: Banging a drum harder makes a bigger vibration and a louder sound.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is a hard drum hit louder than a soft one?'

tutorials.title: Echo
tutorials.body: An echo is sound that bounces off a far surface and comes back to you a moment later. The delay happens because sound takes time to travel there and back. You need a hard surface far enough away to hear the return clearly.
tutorials.example: Shout in a canyon and your voice bounces off the far wall and comes back to you.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why do I hear my voice come back in a canyon?'

tutorials.title: Ultrasound
tutorials.body: Ultrasound is sound too high-pitched for humans to hear, above about 20,000 hertz. It bounces off objects and echoes back, so machines use it to make pictures inside the body or measure distances. Bats and dolphins use it naturally to navigate.
tutorials.example: Doctors use ultrasound to see a baby inside the womb by bouncing high sound waves off it.

tutorials.title: Echolocation
tutorials.body: Echolocation is finding things by sending out sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. The timing and direction of the returning echoes reveal where objects are and how far away. Bats and dolphins use it to hunt and navigate in the dark.
tutorials.example: A bat squeaks in the dark and uses the returning echoes to map insects and walls around it.

tutorials.title: Visible Light
tutorials.body: Visible light is the part of the electromagnetic spectrum our eyes can detect, made of all the colors from red to violet. Each color is light of a different wavelength. Mixed together they look white, and they all travel at the same blazing speed.
tutorials.example: White sunlight is actually all the rainbow colors mixed together.

tutorials.title: Color
tutorials.body: Objects have color because they absorb some light wavelengths and reflect others. The colors that bounce back are what you see. A red apple reflects red light and soaks up the rest; a black object soaks up almost everything, reflecting little.
tutorials.example: A leaf looks green because it reflects green light and absorbs the other colors.

tutorials.title: Dispersion (Prisms)
tutorials.body: A prism splits white light into a rainbow because each color bends by a slightly different amount as it slows down in the glass. Violet bends most and red least, fanning the colors apart. This separating of light is called dispersion.
tutorials.example: Sunlight through a glass prism spreads into a band of rainbow colors on the wall.

tutorials.title: Rainbows
tutorials.body: Rainbows form when sunlight enters raindrops, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again on the way out, splitting into colors. Each raindrop sends one color toward your eyes, and millions of drops together paint the full arc.
tutorials.example: You see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and rain is falling in front of you.

tutorials.title: Infrared
tutorials.body: Infrared is invisible light with wavelengths just longer than red. Warm objects give it off, so cameras that 'see' infrared can spot heat in the dark. TV remotes use infrared to send signals to your television.
tutorials.example: A thermal camera shows people glowing in the dark because their bodies give off infrared.

tutorials.title: Ultraviolet (UV)
tutorials.body: Ultraviolet is invisible light with wavelengths just shorter than violet, carrying more energy than visible light. Too much from the Sun causes sunburn, which is why sunscreen blocks it. Some animals, like bees, can actually see UV patterns on flowers.
tutorials.example: You can get a sunburn on a cloudy day because invisible UV light still reaches your skin.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why can I get sunburned on a cloudy day?'

tutorials.title: How We See
tutorials.body: You see when light bounces off objects, enters your eye, and lands on the retina at the back. Special cells turn that light into signals your brain reads as images. Without light there's nothing to bounce, which is why you can't see in total darkness.
tutorials.example: In a completely dark room you can't see anything because no light is bouncing off objects into your eyes.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why can't I see in a totally dark room?'

tutorials.title: Shadows
tutorials.body: A shadow forms where an object blocks light from reaching a surface. Because light travels in straight lines, it can't bend around solid things, leaving a dark patch shaped like the blocker. Move the light closer and the shadow grows bigger.
tutorials.example: Standing in sunlight, your body blocks the light and casts a shadow on the ground.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is my shadow longer in the evening?'

tutorials.title: Transparent, Translucent, Opaque
tutorials.body: Materials handle light in three ways. Transparent ones like clear glass let light pass straight through so you see clearly. Translucent ones like frosted glass scatter light so things look blurry. Opaque ones like wood block light completely, casting solid shadows.
tutorials.example: You see clearly through a window, blurrily through frosted glass, and not at all through a wooden door.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why can I see through glass but not wood?'

tutorials.title: Resistance
tutorials.body: Resistance is how much a material fights the flow of electric current. High resistance slows current down and often turns electrical energy into heat. Thin or long wires resist more, while thick short ones resist less, like wide pipes letting water flow freely.
tutorials.example: A toaster's wire has high resistance, so it heats up and glows when current pushes through.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a toaster wire get hot?'

triggers: how does a series circuit work
tutorials.title: Series Circuit
tutorials.body: In a series circuit, parts are connected one after another in a single loop, so the same current flows through every part. If one part breaks, the whole circuit stops, like old holiday lights where one dead bulb killed the whole string.
tutorials.example: In old string lights wired in series, one burnt-out bulb made the entire string go dark.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why did old holiday lights all go out if one broke?'

triggers: how does a parallel circuit work
tutorials.title: Parallel Circuit
tutorials.body: In a parallel circuit, parts sit on separate branches, each with its own path for current. If one branch breaks, the others keep working. That's why your home is wired in parallel: one switched-off lamp doesn't darken the whole house.
tutorials.example: Turning off one lamp at home doesn't affect the others because the house is wired in parallel.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why can I turn off one light without the rest going dark?'

triggers: what is the difference between conductors and insulators
tutorials.title: Conductors vs Insulators
tutorials.body: Conductors let electric current flow easily because their electrons move freely; metals like copper are great conductors. Insulators block current because their electrons are locked in place; rubber and plastic are good insulators, which is why wires are coated in them.
tutorials.example: Electrical wires use copper to carry current and plastic coating to keep it safely contained.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why are wires made of metal but covered in plastic?'

tutorials.title: Batteries
tutorials.body: A battery stores chemical energy and turns it into electrical energy on demand. Inside, chemical reactions push electrons out one end and pull them in the other, driving current around a circuit. When the chemicals are used up, the battery goes dead.
tutorials.example: A AA battery powers a toy until its chemicals run out and it needs replacing.

tutorials.title: Magnetism
tutorials.body: Magnetism is a force that pulls or pushes certain metals like iron. Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and like poles repel. The invisible region where the force acts is called a magnetic field.
tutorials.example: Two magnets snap together when opposite poles face, but push apart when same poles meet.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why do two magnets sometimes push apart?'

triggers: how does an electric motor work
tutorials.title: Electric Motors
tutorials.body: An electric motor turns electrical energy into spinning motion. Current flowing through a coil makes it an electromagnet, and a nearby magnet pushes and pulls it so the coil spins around. That spin powers fans, toys, and electric cars.
tutorials.example: A toy car's wheels turn because an electric motor inside converts battery power into spinning motion.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how does electricity make wheels spin?'

tutorials.title: Generators
tutorials.body: A generator is like a motor run backward: instead of using electricity to make motion, it uses motion to make electricity. Spinning a coil near a magnet pushes electrons along the wire, creating current. Power plants spin huge generators to make our electricity.
tutorials.example: A bike's light powers itself with a small generator that spins as the wheel turns.

tutorials.title: Electrical Safety
tutorials.body: Electricity can be dangerous because the human body conducts current, and even a small amount can hurt your heart or burn you. Water makes it worse by helping current flow. That's why you keep electrical things away from water and never poke metal into outlets.
tutorials.example: You should never use a hairdryer near a full sink because water helps electricity reach you.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is electricity dangerous near water?'

triggers: how does a circuit breaker work
tutorials.title: Fuses and Breakers
tutorials.body: Fuses and circuit breakers protect wiring from too much current. If the current gets dangerously high, a fuse melts or a breaker trips, instantly cutting the circuit before wires overheat and start a fire. Breakers can be reset; fuses must be replaced.
tutorials.example: If you plug in too many appliances, a breaker trips and shuts off power to prevent overheating.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a breaker shut off power sometimes?'

tutorials.title: Grounding
tutorials.body: Grounding gives stray electric current a safe path straight into the earth instead of through a person. Appliances have a third prong connected to ground, so if something inside goes wrong, the current rushes harmlessly into the ground rather than shocking you.
tutorials.example: The third prong on a plug is the ground wire, sending dangerous stray current safely into the earth.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what is the third prong on a plug for?'

tutorials.title: Lightning
tutorials.body: Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity. Clouds build up huge amounts of charge as ice and water bump around inside them. When the charge gets strong enough, it leaps as a brilliant bolt to another cloud or the ground, heating the air so fast it bangs as thunder.
tutorials.example: During a storm, charge builds in clouds until it discharges as a lightning bolt to the ground.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'is lightning just giant static electricity?'

tutorials.title: Simple Machines
tutorials.body: Simple machines are basic tools that make work easier by changing the size or direction of a force. The six classics are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and screw. They don't reduce total work, but they spread it out so it feels easier.
tutorials.example: A ramp, a screwdriver, and a seesaw are all simple machines that make a job easier.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how do simple machines make work easier?'

tutorials.title: Levers
tutorials.body: A lever is a stiff bar that pivots on a point called a fulcrum. Pushing down on one end lifts a load on the other. By placing the fulcrum cleverly, a small effort over a long distance can move a heavy load a short distance.
tutorials.example: A seesaw is a lever; sitting farther from the middle lets you lift a heavier friend.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how can a small push lift something heavy?'

tutorials.title: Pulleys
tutorials.body: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it that changes the direction of your pull. Pulling down to lift something up is easier than pushing up. Combining several pulleys lets you lift heavy loads with much less force, spread over more rope.
tutorials.example: A flagpole uses a pulley so you can pull down on the rope to raise the flag up.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is pulling down easier than lifting up?'

tutorials.title: Inclined Plane
tutorials.body: An inclined plane is a ramp that lets you raise something by pushing it up a gentle slope instead of lifting it straight up. It takes less force, but you push over a longer distance, so the total work stays about the same.
tutorials.example: Pushing a heavy box up a ramp into a truck is easier than lifting it straight up.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is a ramp easier than lifting straight up?'

tutorials.title: Wedge
tutorials.body: A wedge is like a moving ramp with a sharp edge that splits or pushes things apart. As you drive it in, it turns your forward push into a strong sideways force. Knives, axes, and door stops are all wedges.
tutorials.example: An axe is a wedge that splits wood by pushing the two sides apart as it sinks in.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how does an axe split wood?'

triggers: what is a screw as a machine
tutorials.title: Screw
tutorials.body: A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a rod into a spiral ridge. Turning it many times pulls it deep into material with great gripping force, while you only have to apply a gentle twisting effort. That's how it holds things tightly together.
tutorials.example: Twisting a screw into wood pulls it in firmly with much less force than hammering.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is a screw stronger than a nail?'

how does a wheel and axle work
tutorials.title: Wheel and Axle
tutorials.body: A wheel and axle is a big wheel attached to a smaller rod (the axle). Turning the large wheel a little makes the axle turn with extra force, or turning the axle spins the wheel fast over a distance. Doorknobs and steering wheels use this idea.
tutorials.example: A doorknob is a wheel and axle; turning the wide knob easily twists the thin shaft inside.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is a wide doorknob easy to turn?'

tutorials.title: Gears
tutorials.body: Gears are toothed wheels that lock together so one turns the next. A small gear driving a big one trades speed for turning force; a big gear driving a small one trades force for speed. That's how bikes and clocks adjust their power and pace.
tutorials.example: Shifting a bike to a low gear makes pedaling easier on a hill by trading speed for force.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a low gear make hills easier on a bike?'

tutorials.title: Air Pressure
tutorials.body: Air pressure is the weight of the atmosphere pressing on everything from all directions. You don't usually feel it because it pushes evenly. Differences in air pressure drive winds and let straws and suction cups work by letting outside air push things along.
tutorials.example: Sucking a straw lowers the pressure inside, so outside air pressure pushes the drink up.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how does a straw actually work?'

tutorials.title: Buoyancy
tutorials.body: Buoyancy is the upward push a liquid or gas gives to objects in it. The fluid pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid the object shoves aside. If that push beats the object's weight, it floats; if not, it sinks.
tutorials.example: A heavy steel ship floats because its hollow shape pushes aside enough water to lift it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a giant metal ship float?'

triggers: why do some things float and others sink
tutorials.title: Density and Floating
tutorials.body: Whether something floats depends on its density compared to the liquid. If an object is less dense than water, it floats; if it's denser, it sinks. Density is how much mass is packed into a space, so a light, spread-out object floats while a heavy, compact one sinks.
tutorials.example: A cork floats but a pebble of the same size sinks because the pebble is denser.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a cork float but a stone sinks?'

tutorials.title: Pendulum
tutorials.body: A pendulum is a weight that swings from a fixed point. Gravity pulls it back toward the middle, so it swings past and back over and over. Surprisingly, the length of the string, not the weight, sets how long each swing takes.
tutorials.example: A grandfather clock uses a swinging pendulum to tick off steady, even seconds.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'does a heavier pendulum swing faster?'

tutorials.title: Speed
tutorials.body: Speed tells you how much distance something covers in a certain time. Go farther in the same time and your speed is higher. We measure it in units like kilometers per hour or meters per second. Average speed smooths out the fast and slow parts of a trip.
tutorials.example: A car covering 60 km in one hour has a speed of 60 km/h.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how do I work out how fast something is going?'

tutorials.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity
tutorials.body: Near Earth's surface, gravity speeds up every falling object at the same rate, about 9.8 meters per second faster each second. Heavy or light, they fall the same if air resistance is ignored. That steady speed-up is why falling feels faster the longer you drop.
tutorials.example: Without air, a feather and a hammer dropped together would hit the ground at the exact same time.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'do heavy things really fall faster than light ones?'

tutorials.title: Weight
tutorials.body: Weight is the force of gravity pulling on an object's mass. It points straight down toward Earth's center. Because it depends on gravity, the same object weighs less on the Moon and would weigh more on a bigger planet, even though its mass never changes.
tutorials.example: A backpack feels heavy because gravity pulls down on all the mass inside it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does my backpack feel heavy?'

tutorials.title: Force
tutorials.body: A force is a push or a pull that can start motion, stop it, change its direction, or change an object's shape. Forces have both strength and direction. You can't always see them, but you see their effects whenever something speeds up, slows, or bends.
tutorials.example: Kicking a ball applies a force that sends it flying in a new direction.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what can a force do to an object?'

tutorials.title: Drag
tutorials.body: Drag is the resisting force a fluid like air or water puts on something moving through it. It grows fast as you speed up and pushes opposite to your motion. Smooth, pointy shapes have less drag, which is why race cars and fish are streamlined.
tutorials.example: A streamlined sports car shape cuts through air with less drag than a boxy truck.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why are fast cars shaped pointy?'

tutorials.title: Thrust
tutorials.body: Thrust is the forward push that drives vehicles like rockets, planes, and boats. It comes from pushing something backward, so by Newton's third law the vehicle is pushed forward in return. Rockets throw hot gas down to thrust themselves up.
tutorials.example: A rocket blasts hot gas downward, and the reaction thrust pushes the rocket up into the sky.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'how does a rocket push itself up?'

tutorials.title: Lift
tutorials.body: Lift is the upward force that holds an airplane in the air. A wing's shape and tilt make air move faster over the top and push more underneath, creating an upward force. When lift beats the plane's weight, it rises.
tutorials.example: An airplane's wings generate lift as air rushes over and under them at takeoff speed.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'what holds a heavy plane up in the air?'

triggers: when is an object in equilibrium
tutorials.title: Equilibrium
tutorials.body: An object is in equilibrium when all the forces on it cancel out, giving zero net force. It can be sitting still or moving at a steady speed in a straight line. Either way, nothing changes its motion because the forces are perfectly balanced.
tutorials.example: A lamp hanging steadily from the ceiling is in equilibrium: gravity down balances the cord's pull up.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'can a moving object be in equilibrium?'

triggers: how does center of mass work
tutorials.title: Center of Mass
tutorials.body: The center of mass is the balance point of an object, where its weight is evenly spread. If you support an object right under its center of mass, it balances. When this point sits over the base, the object is stable; if it tips past the edge, it falls.
tutorials.example: You can balance a ruler on your finger if your finger is right under its center of mass.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why does a tower fall when it leans too far?'

tutorials.title: Stability
tutorials.body: Something is stable when it's hard to tip over, which happens with a low center of mass and a wide base. Tall, top-heavy objects tip easily because a small lean pushes their center of mass past the edge of the base. Race cars are low and wide to stay stable.
tutorials.example: A race car is low and wide so it stays stable and won't tip over in sharp turns.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why are race cars low and wide?'

tutorials.title: Torque
tutorials.body: Torque is the turning power of a force. Pushing farther from the pivot point makes more torque, so it's easier to spin or twist something. That's why a long wrench loosens a tight bolt better than a short one, and why door handles sit far from the hinges.
tutorials.example: A long wrench loosens a stubborn bolt more easily than a short one because it gives more torque.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'why is a long wrench easier than a short one?'

tutorials.title: Weightlessness
tutorials.body: Weightlessness is the floating feeling you get in free fall, when nothing is pushing up against gravity. Astronauts in orbit aren't beyond gravity; they're falling around Earth along with their spacecraft, so there's no support force and everything floats.
tutorials.example: Astronauts float inside the space station because they and the station are both falling around Earth together.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'is there really no gravity in space?'
